claim: The human endometrium experiences repetitive cycles of tissue wounding characterised by piecemeal shedding of the surface epithelium and rapid restoration of tissue homeostasis.
source: The human endometrium experiences repetitive cycles of tissue wounding characterised by piecemeal shedding of the surface epithelium and rapid restoration of tissue homeostasis.
evidence: This is a general statement about endometrial biology that draws from established scientific knowledge and is supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: A novel population of PDGFRb+ mesenchymal stromal cells developed a unique transcriptomic signature in response to endometrial breakdown/repair.
source: Using scRNAseq, we identified a novel population of PDGFRb + mesenchymal stromal cells that developed a unique transcriptomic signature in response to endometrial breakdown/repair.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNAseq data presented in the manuscript showing distinct cell clusters and their gene expression patterns.

claim: PDGFRb+ mesenchymal stromal cells expressed genes usually considered specific to epithelial cells.
source: These cells expressed genes usually considered specific to epithelial cells and in silico trajectory analysis suggested they were stromal fibroblasts in transition to becoming epithelial cells.
evidence: Supported by scRNAseq data showing expression of both mesenchymal and epithelial markers in the F4 cluster.

claim: In silico trajectory analysis suggested PDGFRb+ cells were stromal fibroblasts in transition to becoming epithelial cells.
source: These cells expressed genes usually considered specific to epithelial cells and in silico trajectory analysis suggested they were stromal fibroblasts in transition to becoming epithelial cells.
evidence: Based on computational trajectory analysis (Monocle3) of scRNAseq data showing a differentiation path from fibroblasts to epithelial cells.

claim: Stromal fibroblasts (PDGFRa+) can undergo mesenchyme to epithelial transformation and become incorporated into the re-epithelialised luminal surface.
source: We demonstrated that stromal fibroblasts can undergo a mesenchyme to epithelial transformation and become incorporated into the re-epithelialised luminal surface of the repaired tissue.
evidence: Demonstrated through lineage tracing experiments using Pdgfra-creERT2;Rosa26-tdTm mice showing tdTm+ cells in the luminal epithelium.

claim: This is the first study to discover a novel population of wound-responsive, plastic endometrial stromal fibroblasts that contribute to rapid restoration of an intact luminal epithelium during endometrial repair.
source: This study is the first to discover a novel population of wound-responsive, plastic endometrial stromal fibroblasts that contribute to the rapid restoration of an intact luminal epithelium during endometrial repair.
evidence: This is a summary claim of the study's novelty based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Repetitive injury, inflammation, and fibrosis resulting in disordered tissue architecture is a major cause of morbidity and mortality due to organ failure.
source: Repetitive injury, inflammation, and fibrosis resulting in disordered tissue architecture is a major cause of morbidity and mortality due to organ failure (Greenhalgh et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Greenhalgh et al., 2015.

claim: The endometrium exhibits remarkable resilience in its ability to respond to the monthly wound of menstruation without fibrosis and with a response that is both rapid and scar-free.
source: The endometrium, a complex hormone responsive multicellular tissue, exhibits remarkable resilience in its ability to respond to the monthly wound of 'menstruation' without fibrosis and with a response that is both rapid and scar-free (Garry et al., 2009; Ludwig and Spornitz, 1991).
evidence: Supported by citations to Garry et al., 2009 and Ludwig and Spornitz, 1991.

claim: A critical trigger for menstruation in women is the rapid fall in circulating concentrations of progesterone that occurs as a result of the involution of the ovarian corpus luteum in a non-fertile cycle.
source: A critical 'trigger' for menstruation in women is the rapid fall in circulating concentrations of progesterone that occurs as a result of the involution of the ovarian corpus luteum in a non-fertile cycle (Maybin and Critchley, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Maybin and Critchley, 2011.

claim: Menstruation is considered an inflammatory event with a cascade of changes including an increase in synthesis of pro-inflammatory factors such as prostaglandins, cytokines, and chemokines which is accompanied by infiltration of immune cells of the myeloid lineage.
source: Menstruation is considered an inflammatory event with a 'cascade' of changes including an increase in synthesis of pro-inflammatory factors such as prostaglandins, cytokines, and chemokines which is accompanied by infiltration of immune cells of the myeloid lineage (neutrophils, monocyte/macrophages) (Evans and Salamonsen, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Evans and Salamonsen, 2012.

claim: Increased production of prostaglandins is associated with arteriole vasoconstriction which results in local hypoxia, stabilisation of HIF1alpha and increased expression of genes such as VEGF.
source: Increased production of prostaglandins is associated with arteriole vasoconstriction which results in local hypoxia, stabilisation of HIF1alpha and increased expression of genes such as VEGF (Critchley et al., 2006b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Critchley et al., 2006b.

claim: The Gargett group have identified populations of endometrial mesenchymal stem cells (eMSC) with clonogenic and broad multilineage potential in both human endometrial tissue and menstrual fluid and characterised them as PDGFRB+/CD146+/SUSD2+.
source: The Gargett group have identified populations of endometrial mesenchymal stem cells; eMSC with clonogenic and broad multilineage potential in both human endometrial tissue and menstrual fluid and characterised them as PDGFRB+/CD146+/ SUSD2+ (Gargett et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gargett et al., 2016.

claim: PDGFRB+/CD146+/SUSD2+ cells had a perivascular location and a putative pericyte identity in human endometrial tissue sections.
source: Notably in human endometrial tissue sections these cells had a perivascular location and a putative pericyte identity.
evidence: This is based on observations from the Gargett group's work as cited in the manuscript.

claim: During the first 2 days of menstruation rapid shedding of the luminal portion of the tissue (functional layer) leaves a denuded (basal) stroma interspersed with glandular stumps.
source: During the first 2 days of menstruation rapid shedding of the luminal portion of the tissue (functional layer) leaves a denuded (basal) stroma interspersed with glandular 'stumps'. This phenomenon was beautifully documented in the elegant studies of Ludwig and Spornitz, 1991.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ludwig and Spornitz, 1991.

claim: Ferenczy proposed that new epithelial cells arose from proliferation of intact surface epithelium bordering denuded stroma and the basal glands that were exposed when the functional layer was shed.
source: In the 1970's Ferenczy proposed that new epithelial cells arose from proliferation of intact surface epithelium bordering denuded stroma and the basal glands that were exposed when the functional layer was shed (Ferenczy, 1976b; Ferenczy, 1976a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ferenczy, 1976a and 1976b.

claim: The re-epithelialisation of the human endometrium was rapid (~48 hr) and did not appear to involve mitosis of the epithelial cells.
source: He noted that the re-epithelialisation of the human endometrium was rapid (~48 hr) and did not appear to involve mitosis of the epithelial cells (migration?).
evidence: This is based on Ferenczy's observations as discussed in the manuscript.

claim: Ludwig and Spornitz observed fibrin mesh formation on the denuded surface in the early days of menstruation and growth of an epithelial monolayer in spirals.
source: These mechanisms of epithelial repair were later endorsed by Ludwig and Spornitz, 1991 who also observed fibrin mesh formation on the denuded surface in the early days of menstruation and growth of an epithelial monolayer in spirals which would appear to be consistent with them being associated with the residual stumps of endometrial glands.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ludwig and Spornitz, 1991.

claim: Garry and colleagues found evidence that loss and repair of the surface occur synchronously at different places within the endometrial cavity, a process they called 'piecemeal'.
source: When Garry and colleagues used a more dynamic approach involving pressure-controlled, continuous flow hysteroscopy they found evidence that loss and repair of the surface occur synchronously at different places within the endometrial cavity a process they called 'piecemeal' (Garry et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Garry et al., 2009.

claim: Garry et al. reported epithelial cells of the glands underwent apoptosis and were shed with the decidual tissue mass.
source: They also reported epithelial cells of the glands underwent apoptosis and were shed with the decidual tissue mass.
evidence: This is based on findings from Garry et al. as discussed in the manuscript.

claim: Apoptosis of glandular epithelial cells in carefully dated human endometrium has been documented using staining for cleaved caspase 3 and shown to be high in both late secretory and menstrual phases.
source: Apoptosis of glandular epithelial cells in carefully dated human endometrium has also been documented using staining for cleaved caspase 3 and shown to be high in both late secretory and menstrual phases (Armstrong et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Armstrong et al., 2017.

claim: Baggish et al. proposed that hyperchromatic stromal cells between gland stumps appeared to take part in re-epithelisation by a process simulating metaplasia.
source: This was first proposed in the 1960's by Baggish et al who evaluated sections of menstruating human endometria and noted hyperchromatic stromal cells between gland stumps that appeared to take part in re-epithelisation by a process simulating metaplasia (Baggish et al., 1967).
evidence: Supported by citation to Baggish et al., 1967.

claim: In 2009 Garry et al. reported that the denuded basalis endometrium was rapidly covered with a fibrinous mesh within which new surface epithelial cells were present which appeared to arise from the underlying stroma.
source: Specifically in 2009 the authors reported that the denuded basalis endometrium was rapidly covered with a fibrinous mesh within which new surface epithelial cells were present which appeared to arise from the underlying stroma.
evidence: This is based on findings from Garry et al., 2009 as discussed in the manuscript.

claim: The mouse model used recapitulates key features of human menstruation including vascular breakdown, spatial and temporal hypoxia, cell apoptosis, expression of matrix metalloproteinases and influx of myeloid immune cells.
source: To complement studies on human tissue samples and studies in primates (Brenner et al., 2002; Critchley et al., 2006a) we have used a highly reproducible mouse model that recapitulates key features of human menstruation in response to withdrawal of progesterone including vascular breakdown (vaginal bleeding), spatial and temporal hypoxia, cell apoptosis, expression of matrix metalloproteinases and influx of myeloid immune cells (Armstrong et al., 2017; Maybin et al., 2018; Cousins et al., 2016a; Cousins et al., 2016b; Cousins et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work validating the mouse model.

claim: Restoration of an intact luminal epithelial layer occurs within two days in the mouse model.
source: Importantly, as in the human endometrium (Garry et al., 2009), restoration of an intact luminal epithelial layer occurs within two days (Cousins et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cousins et al., 2014 and comparison to human data from Garry et al., 2009.

claim: In the mouse model, evidence was found for epithelial cell migration and proliferation of residual epithelial cells (Ki67+) but no significant proliferation of basal glands.
source: Consistent with some of the reports on repair processes in human endometrium we found evidence for epithelial cell migration and proliferation of residual epithelial cells (Ki67+) but no significant proliferation of basal glands (Cousins et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cousins et al., 2014.

claim: Kaitu'u-Lino et al. reported that a population of epithelial progenitor cells residing in the basal glands might contribute to postmenstrual repair.
source: Kaitu'u-Lino et al used a mouse model in combination with pulse labelling of cells with BrdU, and reported that a population of epithelial progenitor cells residing in the basal glands might contribute to postmenstrual repair (Kaitu'u-Lino et al., 2010, Kaitu'u-Lino et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kaitu'u-Lino et al., 2010 and 2012.

claim: Stromal cells that co-expressed vimentin (stromal cell marker) and cytokeratin (epithelial cell marker) were found specifically residing in areas denuded of epithelium.
source: In our endometrial repair/menstrual model one of our novel findings was the existence of stromal cells that co-expressed vimentin (stromal cell marker) and cytokeratin (epithelial cell marker) specifically residing in areas denuded of epithelium which suggested to us that stromal cells might be changing their phenotype via MET (Cousins et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cousins et al., 2014.

claim: This is the first time that inducible-Cre lineage tracing approaches in adult mice have been used to explore MET in a model of menstruation.
source: To the best of our knowledge this is the first time that inducible-Cre lineage tracing approaches in adult mice have been used to explore MET in a model of menstruation.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the methodological approach used in the study.

claim: Single-cell sequencing of CD31-/CD45-/GFP+(PDGFRβ+) cells from cycling mice and at 24 and 48 hr after progesterone withdrawal resulted in identification of 8 transcriptionally distinct clusters of GFP+ cells.
source: scRNAseq was used to generate a dataset for each timepoint and these were then integrated for downstream cluster and differential gene expression analysis. This strategy resulted in identification of 8 transcriptionally distinct clusters of GFP + cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by scRNAseq data and visualization in Figure 1B.

claim: Three perivascular populations (V, P1, P2) were identified based on expression of Mcam, Cspg4, Rgs4, Acta2.
source: We identified three perivascular populations (V, P1, P2; expression of Mcam, Cspg4, Rgs4, Acta2) and five fibroblast subpopulations (F1-5; expression of Pdgfra, Cd34, Fbln1/2, Mfap4/5, Col1a1).
evidence: Based on scRNAseq data showing expression of canonical perivascular markers.

claim: Five fibroblast subpopulations (F1-5) were identified based on expression of Pdgfra, Cd34, Fbln1/2, Mfap4/5, Col1a1.
source: We identified three perivascular populations (V, P1, P2; expression of Mcam, Cspg4, Rgs4, Acta2) and five fibroblast subpopulations (F1-5; expression of Pdgfra, Cd34, Fbln1/2, Mfap4/5, Col1a1).
evidence: Based on scRNAseq data showing expression of canonical fibroblast markers.

claim: Cells in all eight clusters expressed mesenchymal markers Pdgfrb, Vim, Des, and Thy1.
source: Importantly, cells in all eight clusters expressed mesenchymal markers Pdgfrb, Vim, Des, and Thy1 (Figure 1C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A(iii)) while no clusters expressed Pecam1 (CD31) or Ptprc (CD45) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A(i-ii)) consistent with the cell isolation strategy employed.
evidence: Supported by scRNAseq data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: No clusters expressed Pecam1 (CD31) or Ptprc (CD45), consistent with the cell isolation strategy employed.
source: Importantly, cells in all eight clusters expressed mesenchymal markers Pdgfrb, Vim, Des, and Thy1 (Figure 1C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A(iii)) while no clusters expressed Pecam1 (CD31) or Ptprc (CD45) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A(i-ii)) consistent with the cell isolation strategy employed.
evidence: Supported by scRNAseq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A confirming absence of endothelial and immune cell markers.

claim: Five mesenchyme subpopulations previously identified in cycling mouse uterine tissue (V, P1, F1-3) were confirmed in the analysis.
source: Analysis of the distribution of these subpopulations in the different datasets (Figure 1D) confirmed the presence of five mesenchyme subpopulations previously identified in cycling mouse uterine tissue (V, P1, F1-3; Kirkwood et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by comparison to previous scRNAseq data from Kirkwood et al., 2021 and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Three additional transcriptionally distinct repair-specific cell clusters were identified: P2 and F4 in 24 hr tissues and F5 in 48 hr tissues.
source: However in tissue recovered at 24 and 48 hr three additional transcriptionally distinct repair-specific cell clusters were identified: P2 and F4 in 24 hr tissues (Figure 1D; green and purple circles respectively) and F5 present in 48 hr tissues (Figure 1D; pink ellipse).
evidence: Supported by scRNAseq data and visualization in Figure 1D showing clusters specific to repair timepoints.

claim: P2 showed a very high degree of similarity to P1 (previously identified as pericytes).
source: Differential gene expression analysis revealed a very high degree of similarity between P1 (previously identified as pericytes) (Kirkwood et al., 2021) and P2 which was specific to 24 hr tissue (Figure 2A).
evidence: Based on differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Unbiased GO analysis of the P2 transcriptome identified functions associated with blood vessel formation and immune cell signalling, characteristic of pericytes.
source: Unbiased GO analysis of the P2 transcriptome identified functions associated with blood vessel formation and immune cell signalling, characteristic of pericytes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D(i)) suggesting a role for these cells in angiogenesis and regulation of the immune system in response to changes in the local environment.
evidence: Based on gene ontology analysis of P2 cluster shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D(i).

claim: Cluster F5 expressed a large number of mitochondrial genes and genes associated with cell death including Casp3, Casp9, Trp53 and Bax.
source: We noted that cluster F5 (specific to 48 hr tissue) expressed a large number of mitochondrial genes and genes associated with cell death including Casp3, Casp9, Trp53 and Bax (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by scRNAseq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: GO analysis of the F5 transcriptome identified functions associated with DNA damage.
source: GO analysis of the F5 transcriptome identified functions associated with DNA damage.
evidence: Based on gene ontology analysis of F5 cluster transcriptome.

claim: F5 represents a cluster of dead/apoptotic cells.
source: Based on this in silico data and the results in our previous study using the same mouse model system that detected high levels of cleaved caspase expression in the stromal compartment at 24 hr (Armstrong et al., 2017) we suggest that F5 represents a cluster of dead/apoptotic cells and it was therefore excluded from further downstream analyses.
evidence: Based on scRNAseq data showing apoptosis markers and previous experimental data from Armstrong et al., 2017.

claim: Cluster F4 had a transcriptomic signature that was distinct from mesenchymal cell populations (F1-3) present in cycling endometrium.
source: Cluster F4 (24 hr tissue) was of particular interest as it had a transcriptomic signature that was distinct from to those of the mesenchymal cell populations (F1-3) present in cycling endometrium (Kirkwood et al., 2021; Figure 2A; red box).
evidence: Supported by differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Unbiased GO analysis of F4 enriched for biological functions associated with endometrial tissue repair including response to wounding, reproductive structure development, response to oxidative stress and regulation of vasculature development.
source: Unbiased GO analysis enriched for biological functions that are associated with endometrial tissue repair including response to wounding, reproductive structure development, response to oxidative stress and regulation of vasculature development.
evidence: Based on gene ontology analysis of F4 cluster shown in Figure 2B.

claim: GO analysis of F4 identified functions including epithelium migration, morphogenesis of a branching epithelium and regulation of epithelial cell migration.
source: Additional functions that were identified included epithelium migration, morphogenesis of a branching epithelium and regulation of epithelial cell migration (Figure 2B).
evidence: Based on gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Cluster F4 was the only mesenchymal cell cluster that expressed markers known to be associated with both definitive mesenchymal (Pdgfrb, Vim) and epithelial (Epcam, Krt18) cell types.
source: Cluster F4 was the only mesenchymal cell cluster that expressed markers known to be associated with both definitive mesenchymal (Pdgfrb, Vim) and epithelial (Epcam, Krt18) cell types (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by scRNAseq data showing co-expression of mesenchymal and epithelial markers in Figure 2C.

claim: F4 was the only cluster that expressed genes associated with both mesenchymal/fibroblast markers and epithelial markers.
source: Comparison across all mesenchymal clusters of the expression of both known canonical mesenchymal/fibroblast markers including Thy1, Cd34, Cdh11, Col1a1, Col3a1, Fbln1, Fbln2, Mfap4, and Mfap5 and epithelial markers such as Krt8, Krt19, Muc1, Muc4, Cd24a, Car2, Sdc4, Alcam, and Cdh1 revealed F4 to be the only cluster that expressed genes associated with both cell types.
evidence: Based on comprehensive gene expression analysis across all clusters.

claim: F4 did not express the full array of keratins and mucins associated with definitive epithelial lineages but preferentially expressed Alcam, Cd24a, Clu, Krt18, and Sdc4.
source: Notably, F4 did not express the full array of keratins and mucins associated with definitive epithelial lineages but preferentially expressed Alcam, Cd24a, Clu, Krt18, and Sdc4 when compared to other mesenchymal clusters (Figure 2D; red box).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: F4 cells may be of an intermediate phenotype and represent cells undergoing a mesenchymal to epithelial transition (MET) but not yet fully committed to a definitive epithelial lineage.
source: We considered this was evidence that these cells may be of an intermediate phenotype and represent cells undergoing a mesenchymal to epithelial transition (MET) but not yet fully committed to a definitive epithelail lineage.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the gene expression patterns observed in F4.

claim: F4 expressed key transcription factors associated with MET/EMT including Cemip, Cited1, Ctnnb1, Grem1, Hmga2, Klf4, and Twist2.
source: This analysis identified that F4 also expressed key transcription factors associated with MET/EMT including Cemip, Cited1, Ctnnb1, Grem1, Hmga2, Klf4, and Twist2 (Figure 2E).
evidence: Based on analysis of MET/EMT-associated genes from MSigDB shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Cells that expressed both GFP and EPCAM were identified in endometrial tissue undergoing active repair (24 hr) specifically in regions where the stromal surface was denuded after decidual shedding and where a new epithelial cell layer was being re-instated.
source: Cells that expressed both GFP and EPCAM were identified in endometrial tissue undergoing active repair (24 hr; Figure 3A (i); white arrows) specifically in regions where (a) the stromal surface was denuded after decidual shedding and (b) a new epithelial cell layer was being re-instated.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Some GFP+EPCAM+ cells persisted in the luminal layer at 48 hr but were not detected in 72 hr tissue.
source: Some GFP + EPCAM + cells persisted in the luminal layer at 48 hr but were not detected in 72 hr tissue (Figure 3A ii, iii).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In control/cycling endometrium expression of the GFP reporter was exclusive to the stromal compartment and epithelial cells were EPCAM+.
source: Consistent with previous data in control/cycling endometrium expression of the GFP reporter was exclusive to the stromal compartment and epithelial cells were EPCAM + (yellow arrows, Figure 3A iv; Kirkwood et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 3A and citation to Kirkwood et al., 2021.

claim: Flow cytometry confirmed the presence of a new population of cells that expressed both GFP and EPCAM at 24 hr with a reduction in their number at 48 hr.
source: Analysis of the same tissues using flow cytometry confirmed the presence of a new population of cells that expressed both GFP and EPCAM at 24 hr with a reduction in their number at 48 hr and levels that appeared comparable to cycling/control tissues in the fully remodelled tissue (72 hr) (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: At 24 hr, GFP+EPCAM+ cells represented ~12.78% of GFP+ cells.
source: Bar plot: quantification of FC data analysing the expression of EPCAM by GFP reporter positive cells in the uterus (%) - control (n=21) 0.53 ± 0.46%; 24 hr (n=30) 12.78 ± 2.49%; 48 hr (n=17) 3.71 ± 1.36%; 72 hr (n=6) 0.96 ± 0.47%; one-way ANOVA, Sidak's multiple comparisons.
evidence: Quantitative flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Bioinformatic analysis combining GFP+ datasets and GFP-EPCAM+ epithelial cell data identified 16 distinct cell clusters.
source: Bioinformatic analysis combining GFP + datasets (cycling/24 hr/48 hr) and GFP-EPCAM + epithelial cell data (cycling/48 hr) identified 16 distinct cell clusters (Figure 4A and C).
evidence: Supported by integrated scRNAseq analysis shown in Figure 4A and C.

claim: Seven of the 16 clusters had a mesenchyme phenotype: three perivascular (V, P1-2), four fibroblast (F1-4).
source: Based on expression of Pdgfrb (Figure 4Bii) and canonical markers (Figure 4D) seven of these had a mesenchyme phenotype: three perivascular (V, P1-2), four fibroblast (F1-4).
evidence: Based on marker gene expression shown in Figure 4B and 4D.

claim: Nine of the 16 clusters expressed classical markers of epithelial cells including Epcam (E1-9).
source: Nine of the clusters expressed classical markers of epithelial cells including Epcam (E1-9) (Figure 4A and B (i, ii), C).
evidence: Based on marker gene expression shown in Figure 4A, B, and C.

claim: The repair-specific fibroblasts (F4) formed a cluster which appeared in close proximity to both fibroblast and epithelial cell clusters but remained distinct from definitive perivascular cells.
source: Notably, the previously identified repair-specific fibroblasts (F4) formed a cluster which appeared in close proximity to both fibroblast and epithelial cell clusters but remained distinct from definitive perivascular cells (V, P1, P2).
evidence: Based on UMAP visualization of integrated scRNAseq data showing spatial relationships between clusters.

claim: A high degree of similarity was observed between the transcriptomic signature of F4 and the definitive epithelial cell clusters E1 and E2.
source: A high degree of similarity was observed between the transcriptomic signature of F4 and the definitive epithelial cell clusters E1 and E2 (Figure 4C, red box, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by heatmap analysis shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Cluster F4 uniquely expressed genes associated with both fibroblast and epithelial lineages.
source: Extended analysis of canonical markers of mesenchymal (perivascular/fibroblast) and epithelial cell types confirmed that cluster F4 uniquely expressed genes associated with both fibroblast and epithelial lineages (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C(i-iv)).
evidence: Supported by comprehensive marker analysis shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The repair-specific mesenchyme cluster F4 expressed genes associated with both luminal (Fxyd4, Gsto1, Plac8, Ctsl, Lgals3, Cited2) and differentiating (Ctnnb1, Krt8, Krt18, Plk2, Basp1, Ptgs2, Olfm1) epithelial cell phenotypes.
source: Notably, the repair-specific mesenchyme cluster F4 also expressed genes associated with both luminal (Fxyd4, Gsto1, Plac8, Ctsl, Lgals3, Cited2) and differentiating (Ctnnb1, Krt8, Krt18, Plk2, Basp1, Ptgs2, Olfm1) epithelial cell phenotypes with no expression of genes considered definitive for glandular epithelium (Foxa2, Cxcl15).
evidence: Based on gene expression analysis of epithelial subtype markers shown in Figure 4E.

claim: F4 had no expression of genes considered definitive for glandular epithelium (Foxa2, Cxcl15).
source: Notably, the repair-specific mesenchyme cluster F4 also expressed genes associated with both luminal (Fxyd4, Gsto1, Plac8, Ctsl, Lgals3, Cited2) and differentiating (Ctnnb1, Krt8, Krt18, Plk2, Basp1, Ptgs2, Olfm1) epithelial cell phenotypes with no expression of genes considered definitive for glandular epithelium (Foxa2, Cxcl15).
evidence: Based on gene expression analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Monocle3 analysis segregated the scRNAseq data into two partitions: one that encompassed the perivascular subsets and one that contained both the fibroblast and epithelial subsets.
source: Monocle3 analysis segregated the scRNAseq data into two partitions: one that encompassed the perivascular subsets; and one that contained both the fibroblast and epithelial subsets.
evidence: Based on Monocle3 trajectory analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: This pattern would be consistent with genetic changes linking fibroblasts and epithelial cells but none between either fibroblasts or epithelial cells and the perivascular clusters.
source: We infer that this would be consistent with a pattern of genetic changes linking fibroblasts and epithelial cells but none between either fibroblasts or epithelial cells and the perivascular clusters (Figure 5A i-ii).
evidence: This is an inference based on the Monocle3 trajectory analysis results.

claim: Monocle3 identified a root within fibroblast cluster F2 with a branch moving through the repair-specific cluster F4 into a root in the epithelial clusters on the border of E1 and E2.
source: Further interrogation of the Monocle data identified a 'root' within fibroblast cluster F2 with a branch moving through the repair-specific cluster F4 into a root in the epithelial clusters on the border of E1 and E2, with subsequent branches moving into other epithelial subsets (Figure 5A iii).
evidence: Based on Monocle3 trajectory analysis shown in Figure 5A iii.

claim: No roots were placed within the F4 cluster (only a trajectory branch), which suggests this population does not have a terminally differentiated phenotype but represents a transitional transcriptional state.
source: No roots were placed within the F4 cluster (only a trajectory branch; Figure 5A i-iii) which further suggests this population does not have a terminally differentiated phenotype, rather it represents a transitional transcriptional state.
evidence: Based on interpretation of Monocle3 trajectory analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: scVelo analysis showed a transition from F2 to F4, with cells in the F4 cluster displaying a positive unspliced/spliced ratio reinforcing their potential for cellular transition towards the epithelial clusters (E1/2).
source: A transition from F2 to F4 was observed, inferring the presence of pseudotemporal dynamics between the two subpopulations, with cells in the F4 cluster displaying a positive unspliced/spliced ratio reinforcing their potential for cellular transition in the direction away from F2 and towards the epithelial clusters (E1/2) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B; red asterisk).
evidence: Based on RNA velocity analysis using scVelo shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: scVelo analysis showed a transition from P1 to P2.
source: Similarly, a transition from P1 to P2 was observed (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B; blue asterisk).
evidence: Based on RNA velocity analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: The transitions within epithelial sub-populations E1/2 appeared to move away from F4 and towards E1 and E2.
source: Notably, the transitions within epithelial sub-populations E1/2 appeared to move away from F4 and towards E1 and E2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B; green asterisk).
evidence: Based on RNA velocity analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: A cellular transition from F1/2/3 through F4 into E1/2 may exist.
source: Taken together, these bioinformatic analyses suggest that a cellular transition from F1/2/3 through F4 into E1/2 may exist.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on Monocle3 and scVelo trajectory analyses.

claim: In the Pdgfra-creERT2/Rosa26-tdTm mouse uterus tdTm expression was detected in cells dispersed throughout the endometrial stromal compartment, but not in cells of the myometrium or luminal/glandular epithelium.
source: In the Pdgfra-creERT2/Rosa26-tdTm mouse uterus tdTm expression was detected in cells dispersed throughout the endometrial stromal compartment, but not in cells of the myometrium or luminal/glandular epithelium (Figure 5D ii).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5D ii.

claim: The tdTm expression pattern in Pdgfra-creERT2/Rosa26-tdTm mice replicated the location of GFPdim stromal fibroblasts in the Pdgfrb-BAC-eGFP mouse uterus.
source: This pattern replicated the location of GFPdim stromal fibroblasts in the Pdgfrb-BAC-eGFP mouse uterus (Figure 5D i)
evidence: Based on comparison of immunohistochemistry patterns between the two mouse lines shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Co-localisation of tdTm and native protein PDGFRα was confirmed in Pdgfra-creERT2/Rosa26-tdTm mice.
source: We confirmed co-localisation of tdTm and native protein PDGFRα (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: tdTm+ cells in Pdgfra-creERT2/Rosa26-tdTm mice did not express CD146.
source: We also confirmed that these tdTm + cells did not express CD146 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) and concluded that the tdTM transgene is specific to PDGFRα+endometrial fibroblasts.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry and flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The tdTM transgene is specific to PDGFRα+ endometrial fibroblasts.
source: We also confirmed that these tdTm + cells did not express CD146 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) and concluded that the tdTM transgene is specific to PDGFRα+endometrial fibroblasts.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple validation experiments including co-localization with PDGFRα and absence of CD146.

claim: In the iNG2-creER/Rosa26-tdTm mouse uterus tdTm was detected in groups of cells dispersed throughout the stromal compartment but not the myometrium or epithelium (luminal/glandular).
source: In the iNG2-creER/Rosa26-tdTm mouse uterus tdTm was detected in groups of cells dispersed throughout the stromal compartment but not the myometrium or epithelium (luminal/ glandular) (Figure 5D iii).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5D iii.

claim: The tdTm pattern in iNG2-creER/Rosa26-tdTm mice was similar to perivascular GFPbright cells in the Pdgfrb-BAC-eGFP mouse uterus.
source: This pattern was similar to perivascular GFPbright cells in the Pdgfrb-BAC-eGFP mouse uterus (Figure 5D (i); Kirkwood et al., 2021), and therefore appeared to represent perivascular cells.
evidence: Based on comparison of immunohistochemistry patterns and citation to Kirkwood et al., 2021.

claim: Co-localisation of tdTm reporter with native NG2 protein was confirmed in iNG2-creER/Rosa26-tdTm mice.
source: To confirm this we co-localised the tdTm reporter with native NG2 protein (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: tdTm+ cells in iNG2-creER/Rosa26-tdTm mice express the canonical pericyte/vSMC marker CD146 but not the endothelial cell marker CD31.
source: We also confirmed they express the canonical pericyte/vSMC marker CD146 but not the endothelial cell marker CD31.
evidence: Based on immunohistochemistry and flow cytometry validation experiments.

claim: Induced tdTm expression in the iNG2-creER/Rosa26-tdTm mouse uterus correctly targets NG2+ perivascular cells (pericytes/vSMC).
source: Taken together, we concluded that induced tdTm expression in the iNG2-creER/Rosa26-tdTm mouse uterus correctly targets NG2 + perivascular cells (pericytes/vSMC).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple validation experiments including co-localization with NG2 and expression of CD146.

claim: In Pdgfra-creERT2/Rosa26-tdTm mice at 24 hr after progesterone withdrawal, a unique population of tdTm+EPCAM+ cells were detected in regions where the decidualised tissue had detached leaving the stromal surface denuded.
source: Notably in the 24 hr tissue a unique population of tdTm + cells that co-expressed the epithelial cell marker EPCAM (tdTm + EPCAM + cells) were detected in two regions one where the decidualised tissue had detached leaving the stromal surface denuded (Figure 6A i-iii; white arrows) and the second population having a phenotype that resembled a new epithelial layer which in some cases was continuous with tdTm-EPCAM + cells (Figure 6A iv; white and yellow arrows respectively).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In Pdgfra-creERT2/Rosa26-tdTm mice at 24 hr, tdTm+EPCAM+ cells were detected having a phenotype that resembled a new epithelial layer which in some cases was continuous with tdTm-EPCAM+ cells.
source: Notably in the 24 hr tissue a unique population of tdTm + cells that co-expressed the epithelial cell marker EPCAM (tdTm + EPCAM + cells) were detected in two regions one where the decidualised tissue had detached leaving the stromal surface denuded (Figure 6A i-iii; white arrows) and the second population having a phenotype that resembled a new epithelial layer which in some cases was continuous with tdTm-EPCAM + cells (Figure 6A iv; white and yellow arrows respectively).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In other regions of Pdgfra-creERT2/Rosa26-tdTm tissue at 24 hr, epithelial cells that did not express tdTM were present.
source: In other regions epithelial cells that did not express tdTM were present (Figure 6A v; yellow arrows).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: A transient population of tdTm+CD90+EPCAM+ cells were detected at 24 hr in Pdgfra-creERT2/Rosa26-tdTm mice which represented ~20% of the reporter+ population.
source: A transient population of tdTm + CD90+EPCAM + cells were detected at 24 hr (red box) which represented ~20% of the reporter + population (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6B-C.

claim: At 24 hr in Pdgfra-creERT2/Rosa26-tdTm mice, tdTm+CD90+EPCAM+ cells represented 19.76 ± 3.24% of tdTm+ cells.
source: Bar plot: quantification of tdTm + CD90+EPCAM + cells at 24/48/72 hr in Pdgfra-creERT2;Rosa26-tdTm uterine tissue, calculated as a frequency of tdTm + cells: Control (n=9): 0.45 ± 0.51%; 24 hr (n=4): 19.76 ± 3.24%; 48 hr (n=9): 0.96 ± 0.64%; 72 hr (n=13): 0.48 ± 0.54%; one-way ANOVA; Tukey's multiple comparisons.
evidence: Quantitative flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Whilst some tdTM+ cells continued to co-express EPCAM at 48 or 72 hr in Pdgfra-creERT2/Rosa26-tdTm mice, these cells were CD90-.
source: Notably whilst some of the tdTM + cells continued to co-express EPCAM at 48 or 72 hr tissue these cells were CD90- (Figure 6C iii-iv).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: In NG2-creER/Rosa26-tdTm mice, cells with a tdTm+CD90+ phenotype were identified in controls and at 24, 48, and 72 hr after induction of repair.
source: When identical analysis methods were applied to tissue recovered from the NG2-creER/Rosa26-tdTm mice cells with a tdTm + CD90+phenotype were identified in controls and at 24, 48, and 72 hr after induction of repair (Figure 6D)
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: In NG2-creER/Rosa26-tdTm mice, no tdTm+EPCAM+ cells were detected nor were any tdTm+ cells present in the epithelial cells at any timepoint.
source: however using sensitive flow cytometry no tdTm + EPCAM + cells were detected nor were any tdTm + cells present in the epithelial cells at any timepoint (Figure 6D–F).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry and immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6D-F.

claim: tdTm+ cells were identified in the luminal epithelium at 48 hr in Pdgfra-creERT2/Rosa26-tdTm mice adjacent to tdTm- epithelial cells.
source: Notably we identified tdTm + cells in the luminal epithelium at 48 hr adjacent to tdTm- epithelial cells (Figure 7A (i-iv); white and yellow arrows respectively).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: tdTm+ and tdTm- epithelial cell populations were detected in uterine tissues at 72 hr in Pdgfra-creERT2/Rosa26-tdTm mice.
source: These two populations of cells were also detected in uterine tissues at 72 hr (Figure 7B iv).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: tdTm expression was not identified in epithelial cell populations at the time of progesterone withdrawal (0 hr) in Pdgfra-creERT2/Rosa26-tdTm mice.
source: Importantly, tdTm expression was not identified in epithelial cell populations at the time of progesterone withdrawal (0 hr; Figure 7B (i); yellow arrows).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Quantification of tdTm reporter protein in EPCAM+ epithelial cells revealed time dependent changes with proportions rising from ~6% at 24 hr to ~17% at 48 hr and ~15% at 72 hr in Pdgfra-creERT2/Rosa26-tdTm mice.
source: Quantification of tdTm reporter protein in EPCAM +epithelial cells revealed time dependent changes with proportions rising from ~6% at 24 hr to ~17% at 48 hr and ~15% at 72 hr (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry quantification shown in Figure 7C.

claim: At 48 hr in Pdgfra-creERT2/Rosa26-tdTm mice, 16.63 ± 2.24% of EPCAM+ cells expressed tdTm.
source: Bar plot: quantification of FC data analysing EPCAM + cells that express tdTm in Pdgfra-creERT2;Rosa26-tdTm uterine tissues 24, 48, and 72 hr following progesterone withdrawal, calculated as a frequency of EPCAM + cells: Control (n=9): 0.75 ± 0.35%; 24 hr (n=4): 3.73 ± 1.81%; 48 h (n=9): 16.63 ± 2.24%; 72 hr (n=13): 13.26 ± 2.42%; one-way ANOVA; Tukey's multiple comparisons.
evidence: Quantitative flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: At 72 hr in Pdgfra-creERT2/Rosa26-tdTm mice, 13.26 ± 2.42% of EPCAM+ cells expressed tdTm.
source: Bar plot: quantification of FC data analysing EPCAM + cells that express tdTm in Pdgfra-creERT2;Rosa26-tdTm uterine tissues 24, 48, and 72 hr following progesterone withdrawal, calculated as a frequency of EPCAM + cells: Control (n=9): 0.75 ± 0.35%; 24 hr (n=4): 3.73 ± 1.81%; 48 h (n=9): 16.63 ± 2.24%; 72 hr (n=13): 13.26 ± 2.42%; one-way ANOVA; Tukey's multiple comparisons.
evidence: Quantitative flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The presence of groups of tdTm+EPCAM+ adjacent to tdTm-EPCAM+ cells in the newly formed luminal epithelium at 48 hr and their persistence at 72 hr is consistent with MET by PDGFRα+ fibroblasts and retention/proliferation of existing epithelial cells both contributing to rapid repair.
source: The presence of groups of tdTm + EPCAM + adjacent to tdTm-EPCAM + cells in the newly formed luminal epithelium at 48 hr and their persistence at 72 hr is consistent with MET by PDGFRα+fibroblasts and retention/proliferation of existing epithelial cells both contributing to rapid repair.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the lineage tracing data showing both tdTm+ and tdTm- epithelial cells.

claim: No tdTm+EPCAM+ cells were detected in NG2-creER/Rosa26-tdTm mice at any timepoint.
source: Importantly we never detected, an equivalent population of tdTm + EPCAM + cells in NG2-creER/Rosa26-tdTm mice at any timepoint (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry and flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mice with stabilisation of Ctnnb1 had smaller uteri, endometrial gland defects, and were infertile.
source: Notably it has previously been reported that mice with stabilisation of Ctnnb1, a gene that plays an important role in Wnt signalling, had smaller uteri, endometrial gland defects, and were infertile (Stewart et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stewart et al., 2013.

claim: Huang et al. used a knock-in strategy with cells expressing LacZ induced by Amhr2-Cre and found labelled cells in both luminal and glandular epithelium post-partum.
source: For example, Huang et al used a knock-in strategy with cells expressing LacZ induced by Amhr2-Cre: in virgin females the reporter was specific to stromal cells but post-partum they found labelled cells in both luminal and glandular epithelium.
evidence: This is a description of findings from Huang et al., 2012 as discussed in the manuscript.

claim: In a study using a SM22a-Cre driver, reporter gene expression (GFP) was detected in the epithelium.
source: In another study using a SM22a-Cre driver, expression of which was reported to be restricted to a subset of CD34 +mesenchymal cells, reporter gene expression (GFP) was also detected in the epithelium (Yin et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yin et al., 2019.

claim: Ghosh et al. questioned whether epithelial cells expressing reporter proteins in the adult endometrium arose from MET or were induced at a time when cells had meso-epithelial characteristics.
source: Specifically, Ghosh et al conducted a comprehensive examination of embryonic and adult reproductive tracts using LacZ reporter lines driven by promoters for the genes Amhr2, Sm22, Cspg4, Thy1 and Pdgfrß all of which are expressed in mesenchyme. They specifically questioned whether epithelial cells expressing reporter proteins in the adult endometrium arose from MET or were induced at a time when cells had meso-epithelial characteristics.
evidence: This is a description of the work and conclusions from Ghosh et al., 2020.

claim: Ghosh et al. attributed epithelial expression in adult epithelial cells to activation of the promoters during embryonic life ruling out MET in adult cycling mice.
source: In all cases, they attributed epithelial expression in adult epithelial cells to activation of the promoters during embryonic life ruling out MET in adult cycling mice (Ghosh et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ghosh et al., 2020.

claim: The half-life of eGFP protein in vivo in cancer was reported to be ~15 hr.
source: This would be consistent with reports that eGFP protein was engineered to have increased fluorescence and slower turnover in vivo Zhao et al., 1999; although the half-life of the protein varies in different cell models a paper exploring in vivo expression in cancer reported it to be ~15 hr (Danhier et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Zhao et al., 1999 and Danhier et al., 2015.

claim: Queckborner et al. subtyped two populations of perivascular/pericyte cells with different expression levels of MY11D and CSPG4.
source: Queckborner and colleagues focused their analysis cells from 3 donors obtained during in the proliferative phase of their menstrual cycle (6864 cells) using a protocol that enriched for stromal cells (Queckbörner et al., 2021). They subtyped two populations of perivascular/pericyte cells with different expression levels of MY11D and CSPG4 both of which we have previously mapped to perivascular populations in the mouse endometrium (Kirkwood et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a description of findings from Queckbörner et al., 2021 as discussed in the manuscript.

claim: Queckborner et al. subtyped the stromal fibroblasts into 10 closely related clusters of fibroblasts and concluded that the markers for progenitor cells were not specific enough.
source: They subtyped the stromal fibroblasts into 10 closely related clusters of fibroblasts and concluded that the markers for progenitor cells were not specific enough.
evidence: This is a description of findings from Queckbörner et al., 2021.

claim: Cao et al. identified two subclusters in cultured cells from the menstrual phase with the larger cluster having high expression of PDGFRβ/PDGFRα consistent with a fibroblast identity.
source: Cao et al focused their attention on the perivascular cell population performing sequence analysis of CD140b+CD146+ (eMSC) cells isolated from menstrual phase (days 2–3) and secretory phases (n=3 women in each group Cao et al., 2021). They identified two subclusters in cultured cells from the menstrual phase with the larger cluster having high expression of PDGFRβ/PDGFRα consistent with a fibroblast identity.
evidence: This is a description of findings from Cao et al., 2021.

claim: Cao et al. concluded that cell transcriptomes had been influenced by cell culture which may compromise attempts to compare between in vitro and in vivo data.
source: When they compared their data to the Wang dataset they noted significant changes in gene expression patterns and concluded that the cell transcriptomes had been influenced by cell culture which may compromise attempts to compare between in vitro and in vivo data.
evidence: This is a description of conclusions from Cao et al., 2021.

claim: Wu et al. identified a stromal cell subcluster enriched for SFRP4 which provided a positive stimulus to regeneration in a rat endometrial injury model.
source: In contrast, we did find some homologies within the dataset published by Wu et al., 2022 whose analysis included single-cell sequencing of full thickness endometrium from the proliferative and secretory phases (no menstrual tissue). Their stromal cell subclusters included one enriched for SFRP4 which they also showed provided a positive stimulus to regeneration in a rat endometrial injury model.
evidence: This is a description of findings from Wu et al., 2022.

claim: Comparison with mouse datasets identified Sfrp4 expression was highest in F2 and F4 populations, very low in F1/F3 and absent from the epithelial cells.
source: Comparison with our own datasets identified Sfrp4 expression was highest in our F2 and F4 populations, very low in F1/F3 and absent from the epithelial cells: two of the factors secreted by the SFRP4 cells were also higher in the mouse F4 than other cell clusters (PENK, GLIPR1).
evidence: Based on comparison of the current study's scRNAseq data with published data from Wu et al., 2022.

claim: Two factors secreted by the SFRP4 cells (PENK, GLIPR1) were higher in the mouse F4 than other cell clusters.
source: Comparison with our own datasets identified Sfrp4 expression was highest in our F2 and F4 populations, very low in F1/F3 and absent from the epithelial cells: two of the factors secreted by the SFRP4 cells were also higher in the mouse F4 than other cell clusters (PENK, GLIPR1).
evidence: Based on gene expression analysis in the current study's scRNAseq data.

claim: Wu et al. found the SFRP4 cells to be distinct to putative progenitors identified as SUSD2+ which were enriched in the perivascular population.
source: Whilst further work is needed to validate whether a population equivalent to F4 is present in the menstrual endometrium looking for SFRP4 cells might provide a useful starting point and it is also notable that the authors found the SFRP4 cells to be distinct to putative progenitors identified as SUSD2 + which were enriched in the perivascular population.
evidence: This is a description of findings from Wu et al., 2022.

claim: The cell type involved in MET is a PDGFRα+ stromal cell and not the NG2+ pericytes.
source: In summary, we describe novel data and new datasets that show MET can contribute to the rapid scar-free healing of the endometrial luminal epithelium when this occurs in response to an endometrial 'wound' at the time of menstruation. The cell type involved in this MET is a PDGFRα+stromal cell and not the NG2 + pericytes.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the lineage tracing experiments comparing Pdgfra-creERT2 and iNG2-creER mice.

claim: MET can contribute to the rapid scar-free healing of the endometrial luminal epithelium in response to an endometrial wound at the time of menstruation.
source: In summary, we describe novel data and new datasets that show MET can contribute to the rapid scar-free healing of the endometrial luminal epithelium when this occurs in response to an endometrial 'wound' at the time of menstruation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental data presented in the study.
